lines.note: The gloss is not loyal, Chǔ narazu, and the Portuguese names disservices. Correct the draft's Chô to the visible u with caron; Fu- starts the following example.

runs.text: Peſſoa que fez, ou faz al-

lines.note: Completes Fuchǔno mono, a disloyal person who has done or does an injury or disservice. The damaged round letter in Peſſoa is o, not the draft's c; al- continues below.
Completes algũ agrauo and the alternative disservice. Preserve the nasal abbreviation and the positional u in agrauo rather than modernizing the Portuguese.
Xiruxi arazu denotes absence of a sign or result. The visible r corrects the draft's atazu; the definition continues with effect on the next row.
The example says that despite praying there was no result. The concessive Inoredomo and the ensuing Portuguese explanation agree; preserve the caron in fucǒnari.

runs.text: mais deprecaçoẽs que fazião não auia effeito.

lines.note: Completes the statement that however much they prayed, there was no effect. The final word has ff, not fſ; preserve the historical nasal-mark placement in deprecaçoẽs.

runs.text: Arte de tanger, ou cantar ao modo de

lines.note: The term denotes the art of playing or singing in the Japanese manner. The long-vowel mark and final unaccented co distinguish this headword from adjacent Fucǒ entries.

runs.text: Iapão. ¶ Item, Liuro ondeſe trata deſta

lines.note: Completes the Japanese manner and adds a book treating that musical art. Retain the tightly printed ondeſe and the historical Liuro spelling.
Closes the second sense, a book on this art. The short continuation is fully present and carries no additional headword at the right edge.
Xitagauazu means not obeying; the Portuguese first specifies disobedience to a parent. Restore the short s in Desobediencia and the visible comma after pay.
The example contrasts duties to one's lord and father. Correct Qinino to Qimino, the historical kimi no form; the scan's middle m supports the lord gloss below.

runs.text: mito nari, chichino tameniua fucǒno co-

lines.note: The person becomes disloyal toward the lord and an unfilial child toward the father. Preserve mito nari and the physical co- break, which continues the child expression below.

runs.text: to naru beqinite ſoro aida, &c. Taif.

lines.note: Completes the Japanese quotation with beqinite soro aida, not the draft's boqinite. Taif. is the source citation, retained in roman with its period and flagged for whole-word typeface review.

runs.text: Lib. 26. Por quanto pera com o ſenhor

lines.note: Specifies book 26 of the cited work and begins the Portuguese rendering concerning the lord. The citation number and Portuguese remain within the printed italic passage.

runs.text: era desleal, & pera com o pay deſobediente,

lines.note: The translation contrasts disloyalty to the lord and disobedience to the father. Correct deſobeciente to deſobediente, supported by the d ascender and the Japanese contrast.

runs.text: &c. Item, Deſobediencia pera com o ſe-

lines.note: Closes the quotation and adds disobedience toward a lord or master as another use. Preserve the long ſ and the explicit ſe- break.
Completes senhor and the alternative master. This continuation finishes the disobedience entry rather than introducing the separate misfortune homonym below.
Saiuai narazu means lacking good fortune; the Portuguese gives misfortune or little luck. Retain the baseline's visible Des dita division instead of normalizing it to a modern joined form.
Completes the little-fortune definition. The final S. is a separate written-language label, not an extra word within the Portuguese noun phrase.

runs.text: Desobediente ao pay, ou mãy, ou ao

lines.note: The adjectival form describes disobedience toward parents or a superior. Correct the draft's Detobediente to the visible short-s Desobediente.
Completes the list of authorities with lord and master. Preserve the ampersand and the historical long-s forms rather than regularizing the coordination.
Tomi tattoxi combines wealth and high standing; the Portuguese gives prosperity and abundance. The q belongs to the historical representation of the Japanese compound.
Completes abundancia, then illustrates prospering or becoming wealthy with Fucqi suru. The Japanese verb expression remains outside the italic Portuguese.
Adds enrichment and introduces the compound with flourishing or increase. Preserve the caron in fanjǒ and the printed division Proſperi-dade.

runs.text: dade, & propagação dalgũa caſa, ou familia.

lines.note: The compound concerns prosperity and the propagation of a household or family. Correct the draft's false split da lgũa to the visible dalgũa.

runs.text: Veſtido: poſto que ſe não vſa aſsi ſe não

lines.note: Fucu is clothing, but the explanation restricts its use without an honorific or compound. Native enlargement resolves aſsi, with one long and one short s, rather than the draft's double-s ligature.

runs.text: com algũa particula de honra, ou compoſição.

lines.note: Completes the usage restriction: an honorific element or compound is needed. This grammatical explanation should not be mistaken for an additional clothing sense.
The example uses honorific go- and the giving verb for a king or lord bestowing clothing. Rey is entirely Portuguese and italic; the draft incorrectly excluded ey from the italic span.
Completes the act of a king or another lord giving a garment. Correct oa to the visible ou; preserve the single Portuguese sentence across the break.
This homonym means good fortune and prosperity, rather than clothing. The following row qualifies these as benefits sought from divine beings.

runs.text: que ſe pedem a os Camis, ou Fotoques. Vt,

lines.note: The prosperity is requested from kami or buddhas. Camis and Fotoques occur within Portuguese prose and are flagged as complete embedded terms, irrespective of their current italic style.
The alternatives are asking or praying for good fortune. Preserve the circumflex in cô and the printed separation de pre- before the continuation caçoẽs.
Completes the petitions for temporal goods. Retain the historical joined temporaaes, including its doubled a, and the nasal-mark placement in caçoẽs.

runs.text: Hum certo peixe que ſe co-

lines.note: The alternative names refer to a poisonous fish, recognizable as fugu from the entry and explanation. Preserve fucutǒ and the physical co-me division; this is historical description, not preparation advice.

runs.text: me en Xiru tirada a peçonha que tem.

lines.note: The historical gloss says the fish is eaten in soup after removal of its poison. Xiru is an embedded Japanese term; its capital has an ambiguous slope, so the whole italic word is flagged for human font review.
Farano yamai identifies an abdominal illness. Correct doerça to doença using the n and cedilla; retain the headword's historical vowel marking rather than deriving it from modern pronunciation.

runs.text: com que incha a barriga, & ſe torna a còr

lines.note: The historical illness description gives abdominal swelling and a change of complexion. Native enlargement and the second pass confirm a grave over the o in còr; retain that printed accent without substituting a modern disease name.
Completes the complexion description as green and yellow. The long-s/t combination in roſto is visible; retain the historical colour description without substituting a disease name.
Farano vchi explains the interior of the belly. The final long vowel is marked with a caron, and the Portuguese noun continues across barri-ga.
Completes belly or stomach and begins an example of abdominal illness. Preserve Fucuchǔqeni and the unhyphenated go/zaru division; the long-s/t shape in eſtamago is visible.
Completes gozaru and gives the alternative that the abdomen is unwell. Preserve the grave-marked varù and the long-s form in the Portuguese Eſtar.

runs.text: doente da barriga, ou de camaras. ¶

lines.note: Explains being ill in the belly or suffering bowel trouble, using historical camaras. The paragraph starts another Fucuchǔ example, physically divided at Fu-.
The example says the abdominal condition has not settled. Retain the visible Portuguese division a cabar and the tight deſe rather than silently regularizing their spacing.

runs.text: temperar a barriga que anda deſtemperada.

lines.note: Completes the description of a still-disordered abdomen failing to regain balance. Remove the false OCR split inside deſtemperada; the full printed word is visible.
This headword denotes good, fertile land. Correct feruil to fertil from the visible t; preserve the Japanese g rather than substituting the next entry's j.
Saiuaino coto means a fortunate matter or good event. Restore the worn a in Saiuaino, omitted by the draft's Siuaino, and retain the physical pro- break.
Completes prosperidade and closes the good-fortune entry. The full short final row is present; the surrounding bottom margin contains no additional body line.
Tomeru fito identifies a wealthy person. Correct the spurious i after initial F in Fiucujin; the damaged F and following u align with Fucujin and the Portuguese wealthy/prosperous gloss.
The verb means putting food into the mouth; the abbreviated paradigm is retained. The scan has na boca, correcting the draft's no boca.
The example explicitly puts food into the mouth and refers to the same definition. Restore the comma after Vt and the period after Idem from the visible punctuation.

runs.text: Poſto que o ordinario modo de falar he,

lines.note: The Portuguese usage note says the ordinary expression is the alternative beginning Cu-. This alternative is embedded after he in Portuguese prose, unlike the separate examples below.
Completes Cucume, uru, then begins the informing/speaking sense with two Japanese alternatives. Preserve the paragraph boundary and the explicit fu- split in mǒxi fucumuru.
Completes the second alternative and explains saying or informing someone. Alguem is printed without a modern accent; no honorific expansion is added to the canonical text.

runs.text: Hũa certa iguaria feita de hum

lines.note: The scan clearly has Fucumadai with a, although its alphabetical position suggests Fucumedai. The supplied NINJAL Entry Words Data of Nippojisho (v202510, Hideyuki Ohshima with Taichi Aida, CC BY 4.0; https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html) also reports the suspected printing error; retain this copy's a.

runs.text: peixe como pargo ſeco, & moido ſem as

lines.note: The dish is made from a fish resembling sea bream, dried and ground. Preserve the historical moido and the conjunction before the deboning qualification below.
Completes the statement that the fish is prepared without its bones. The short continuation belongs to the dish Fucumadai and has no further text at the right.
Vomoteuo vouô means covering the face; the Portuguese describes concealing it. Restore the worn e in Vomoteuo rather than the draft's a; retain the circumflex in vouô.

runs.text: ou cobrir o roſto pera que não ſeja conhecido,

lines.note: Explains covering the face to avoid recognition. Preserve the historical pera and the long-s forms rather than modernizing the phrasing.
The examples mean making or letting down a face covering. Correct Facumenuo to the visible Fucumenuo; retain taruru as the printed alternative, not an inferred modern form.
Refers both face-covering examples back to the same definition. This short row closes the entry before the new verb describing holding something in the mouth.
The verb means holding something in the mouth. Restore the visible tilde in ũda and read algũa rather than algũs; these marks are supported by the scan as well as the inflection and grammar.
The first figurative example is holding joy within oneself. The Portuguese gloss begins rejoicing inwardly and continues across the printed inte- break.
Completes inwardly and introduces harboring sadness. The new Portuguese Eſ- continues into the next row, preserving the physical lineation between the two examples.
Completes being very sad, then introduces a contained smile or glad expression. Preserve the long-s/t form in triſte and the new Eſ- continuation.

Explains being glad or showing a glad face, then starts Vramiuo, harboring resentment. The r after V is severely worn; residual ink and the following resentment gloss support restoration, which is flagged.
Completes Vramiuo fucumu, harboring an inward grievance. The Portuguese explicitly confirms resentment, supporting the damaged r restored on the preceding physical row.
The example concerns harboring ill intent or a bad disposition. Acuxin is the evil-heart term; the following row supplies the person toward whom it is directed.

Completes ill will toward someone and begins harboring anger. The worn glyph after d is the lower remnant of o, giving Iqidouoriuo. NINJAL's transcription of the contemporary Amakusa Heike, p. 41 line 22, independently attests iqidouori: https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/amhk/amhk-r-001.html . The source corroborates the word, not this copy's individual damaged glyph.
Completes fucumu and describes being very angry and hateful. Retain the unaccented odio and the physical division of the Japanese verb.
The example describes a sacrament containing sweetness or delight. Preserve voſazzuqe, the Christian usage of the giving/granting term, and the Sacra- break.

runs.text: mento que encerra em ſi grande goſto.

lines.note: Completes sacramento and explains that it contains great delight within itself. Restore the word boundary after ſi and the visible long-s/t shape in goſto.
The dictionary explicitly prefers Fucujin over Fucunin for a rich person. This is a lexical preference statement, not a licence to replace the headword; preserve the abbreviation Homẽ.
The transitive verb means causing something to swell or grow. Preserve the abbreviated paradigm and the printed cre-cer division.
Completes causing growth and gives the example of puffing out one's cheeks. The circumflex in Fô is visible and is retained, distinct from the carons elsewhere.

The cheek example is followed by causing buns or bread to rise. Páouo is wholly within the Japanese example; enlargement shows an acute-like mark above a, retained provisionally rather than normalized to nasal ã. Its exact accent remains uncertain.
Completes the causative example and describes making the buns rise. Mangiùs is embedded in the Portuguese explanation and is flagged for whole-word font review; retain crecer without adding s.

runs.text: Pão com vinho doce de Iapão, formento, &c.

lines.note: Continues the historical explanation of raising bread using sweet Japanese wine or leaven. The mark after Iapão is a comma, not the draft's period; retain the printed formento.
The intransitive counterpart describes something swelling. Preserve the historical ǒda past-form notation, even though it differs from a modern expected nasal past ending.
Completes growing in the previously described way. The definition connects this intransitive verb with the preceding causative entry without changing either paradigm.
The term denotes a preparation of lightly cooked limpets. Preserve Fucurairi and the historical culinary word Tempera, rather than replacing them with a modern dish name.
The example specifies an oyster version of the preparation. The whole Portuguese Tempera is italic, correcting the draft's isolated roman T; the Japanese example remains roman.
Completes the description of oysters cooked lightly. Preserve leuemente with positional u and its connection to the preceding preparation.
This verb means puffing up or swelling. The historical ruru paradigm is preserved; the following paragraph gives bread rising as an additional application.
Adds the rising or leavening of bread as a sense of Fucure. Preserve the nasalized pão and the historical Leuedarſe spelling.
The term denotes an ornamental metal edging or band, glossed by covering. Correct centa to the visible cinta; the circumflex in Vouô is clear.

runs.text: ou outro metal com que ſe orna algũa couſa.

lines.note: The decorative edging may be gold or another metal used to adorn an object. Retain the nasal abbreviation in algũa and the original relative-clause construction.
Farauo tatçuru is the historical belly-raising idiom for anger. The Portuguese gives vexation or anger, with a visible long-s/t form in Agaſtamento.
The example means becoming angry or vexed. Preserve the long-vowel marking and the long ſ in both the Japanese verb and Portuguese gloss.
The owl headword has a circumflex, unlike the unaccented bag and mother homonyms below. Preserve the old Portuguese Curuja rather than changing it to coruja.
The Japanese is Fucuro, a bag, with r rather than the draft's t. The Portuguese Suco is retained provisionally from the aligned draft: Saco is expected, but the worn vowel looks u-like in this copy.
This homonym means mother; the usage note gives the usual honorific form beginning Vofu-. That form is embedded in the Portuguese explanation and continues on the next row.

runs.text: , & entre molheres poſto que tambem en

lines.note: Completes Vofucuro and the note that it is used among women, though also among other people. The comma remains in the italic continuation; preserve the unhyphenated en/tre break.
Completes entre outras peſſoas, broadening the usage beyond women. Restore the two long-s forms from the scan instead of the draft's erroneous t.

The entry denotes an unstitched or opened seam and explicitly prefers Focorobi. Preserve both lexical forms; the separate Fucu- catchword below is furniture, whose missing hyphen is reported separately.
